title: At-Home Strep Test: Accuracy, How to Use It, and When to See a Doctor
summary: Can you test for strep at home? A pediatrician explains what at-home rapid strep tests can and can't tell you, how to swab correctly, and when to call a doctor.

Yes, rapid strep tests can be used at home, but not the way a COVID test can. They are prescription devices, so a clinician has to order one, and no at-home strep test has FDA clearance for over-the-counter sale yet (as of August 2026). Used correctly, a rapid test catches about 6 out of every 7 cases of strep. That means a positive result is your cue to call your pediatrician for treatment, and a negative result in a child might not be the final word. ## Key Takeaways


- Rapid strep tests can be used at home, but they are prescription devices. There is no FDA-cleared over-the-counter version yet (as of August 2026).
- Used correctly, they catch about 6 out of every 7 cases of strep, so a test can miss it.
- A negative result in a child does not always rule out strep. A Blueberry pediatrician can help guide your next steps.
- A positive result is usually right, so call your pediatrician for treatment.
- Symptoms alone cannot diagnose strep. A cough, runny nose, or pink eye usually points to a virus.
- Treating strep prevents rheumatic fever, and untreated strep can also lead to abscesses and ear or sinus infections.
- A Blueberry telemedicine visit can help you sort out your child's symptoms and next steps.


## Can you test for strep at home?


Yes, rapid strep tests can be used at home, but a clinician has to order one, because they are prescription devices in the United States. A test kit holds a soft throat swab and a test strip or cassette, plus small tubes of liquid that react with the sample. Results usually appear in about 5 to 10 minutes, depending on the brand.


A rapid strep test looks for proteins on the surface of group A strep, the bacteria that cause strep throat. It does not grow the live bacteria the way a lab culture does. That is why it is fast, and also why it can miss a real infection if the swab does not pick up enough of the sample.


## Are at-home strep tests available over the counter (OTC)?


Not yet. As of August 2026, the FDA has not cleared any rapid strep test for over-the-counter home use. So you cannot pick one up the way you would grab a COVID or flu test.


Rapid strep tests are prescription devices. That means a licensed clinician has to order one. Kits you may see for sale online are made for doctors' offices and clinics, not for buying on your own. A listing that says "FDA approved for home use" is marketing language, not a regulatory approval. At least one company is working toward the first FDA-cleared home version, but it has not been cleared yet.


The route that actually exists is a clinician ordering the test for you. That is exactly how Blueberry works, and it is why parents can get a real test without guessing at a pharmacy shelf.


## Where can I buy an at-home strep test?


Because rapid strep tests are prescription devices, the reliable way to get one is to have a clinician order it for you, not to buy a single kit off a shelf. Major pharmacies do not sell single-pack home strep tests to consumers; their strep testing happens in the clinic. You will find kits on online marketplaces, but those are professional-use devices sold outside the setting they were cleared for, not FDA-cleared home tests, whatever the listing says.


You have a few real options:


- In-clinic testing. A pediatrician's office, urgent care, or retail clinic can swab and test your child in person.
- The Blueberry route. A Blueberry pediatrician can order a rapid strep test and walk you through using it at home.


With a Blueberry membership, a pediatrician can order a rapid strep test for your child and tell you how to use it at home. The test is prescribed and purchased separately from your medical kit, and it can take a few days to arrive. So if your child is sick right now, start a visit and your pediatrician will tell you the fastest way to get them tested. The kit does not ship overnight, so joining before someone is sick is the difference between testing tonight and waiting.


## What is strep throat?


[Strep throat](https://www.blueberrypediatrics.com/health-tips/strep-throat-a-complete-guide-for-parents) is a sore throat caused by group A strep bacteria. It is most common in children 5 through 15 years old (CDC). The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) notes it peaks around 7 or 8 years of age. It is not the same as most[sore throats](https://www.blueberrypediatrics.com/health-tips/sore-throat-symptoms-causes-treatment) , which are caused by viruses and get better on their own.


Common signs of strep throat include a sudden sore throat, pain with swallowing, and fever (CDC). The tonsils may be swollen with white patches or pus. The glands in the front of the neck can be tender and swollen. Some children get tiny red spots on the roof of the mouth. Strep usually does not come with a cough or runny nose.


## Strep throat vs. a viral sore throat: how to tell the difference


You cannot tell strep from a virus by symptoms alone, but the pattern of symptoms can point you in the right direction before a test. Most sore throats are viral. In fact, only about 3 in 10 children with a sore throat actually have strep (CDC).


The table below shows the clues pediatricians weigh. Certain "viral" signs are especially useful: CDC says children with a cough, runny nose, hoarse voice, mouth ulcers, or pink eye usually do not need a strep test at all.


Sign or symptom More likely strep More likely a virus


Sudden sore throat with pain swallowing Common Less typical


Fever Common Sometimes


Swollen tonsils with white patches Common Less typical


Tender, swollen neck glands Common Less typical


Cough Usually absent Common


Runny nose Usually absent Common


Hoarse voice Usually absent Common


Pink eye (conjunctivitis) Usually absent Common


Even with this pattern, symptoms cannot diagnose strep by themselves, in a parent's hands or a pediatrician's. That is what a test is for. If your child has clear viral signs like a cough and runny nose, a strep test is usually not needed.


## How accurate are at-home rapid strep tests?


Rapid strep tests catch about 6 out of every 7 children who have strep, which means about 1 in 7 cases is missed. That comes from a large 2016 Cochrane review of 98 studies and more than 100,000 children (Cohen and colleagues). In plain terms, out of 100 children who really have strep, a rapid test finds about 86 and misses about 14.


The better news is on the other side: rapid tests rarely call strep when it is not there. A positive result is usually correct, which is why a positive means you can call your pediatrician for treatment without waiting for a culture.


Those accuracy numbers come from studies where nurses and doctors took the swab in a clinic. No published study has measured how well a rapid test works when a parent does the swabbing at home. Since a good swab is what drives accuracy, and a parent swabbing a squirming child is the hardest case, that 86 percent is a best case for home use, not a promise. It is one more reason a negative result in a child should not be the end of the story.


## How does a rapid strep test differ from a throat culture?


A rapid strep test gives a fast answer in minutes. A throat culture is a lab test that grows the bacteria over 1 to 2 days. It catches a few cases the rapid test misses. Doctors call the culture the gold standard because it is more thorough. The trade-off is time.


Feature Rapid strep test Throat culture


What it is A quick test for strep proteins (antigens) A swab grown in a lab


Time to result About 5 to 10 minutes About 1 to 2 days


How many cases it catches About 6 out of 7 The most thorough test available


Best use A fast answer; a positive is reliable Confirming a negative rapid test in a child


In children, pediatricians often confirm a negative rapid test with a throat culture (AAP). That back-up culture is how they avoid missing the roughly 1 in 7 cases a rapid test can overlook.


## How to use an at-home strep test correctly (step-by-step)


The part you control most is the swab, and a good swab is what makes the test reliable. A rapid strep test does not collect saliva. The swab has to firmly touch both tonsils and the back wall of the throat. (If the tonsils have been removed, swab where they used to be.) Keep the swab off the tongue, cheeks, lips, and teeth. Thinking "get some spit" is the wrong picture. A tongue swab is a classic reason a test misses strep.


Follow the instructions that come with your specific kit, since timing and steps vary by brand. In general:


1. Read your kit's insert first, and set out everything you need.
2. Use good light and a clean spoon handle or tongue depressor to hold the tongue down.
3. Firmly rub the swab over both tonsils and the back wall of the throat. A brief gag is normal and is a sign the swab reached the right spot.
4. Avoid touching the tongue, cheeks, lips, and teeth with the swab.
5. Start the timer and read the result inside the time window on the insert. Reading too early or too late can both give a wrong answer.
6. Follow your kit's insert on how to read a faint line, since kits differ on what a faint line means.


The most common fixable reason a home test misses strep is a swab that did not reach the right spot. Slow down, get good light, and touch both tonsils and the back of the throat.


## What if the at-home strep test is negative?


A negative home test does not rule out strep in a child, so pediatricians often confirm a negative rapid test with a throat culture. Remember that a rapid test misses about 1 in 7 cases, and a swab taken at home may miss more.


A back-up culture is simply the same kind of swab, grown in a lab for a day or two to give the bacteria a chance to show up. In children older than 3, CDC guidance supports confirming a negative rapid test with a culture. If your child has strep-like symptoms and a negative home test, it might still be strep. A Blueberry pediatrician can help guide your next steps, especially if the sore throat, fever, or swollen glands continue.


> Call your pediatrician if your child has a sore throat that persists (not one that goes away after their first drink in the morning) - whether or not it is accompanied by fever, headache, stomachache or extreme fatigue.
>
>
> American Academy of Pediatrics, HealthyChildren.org


## What happens if the strep test is positive?


A positive home test is usually right, so the next step is to call your pediatrician, who can start treatment. Because rapid tests rarely call strep when it is not there, a positive result does not need a confirming culture the way a negative one does.


There is one wrinkle worth knowing. Some healthy children carry group A strep in their throat without being sick. If a carrier catches a cold, a strep test can turn positive even though a virus is causing the sore throat. So a positive home test is a reason to call your pediatrician, and the pediatrician, not the kit, decides whether strep is really what is making your child sick.


## Why treating strep matters


Treating strep is about preventing rare but serious problems, and the full picture has two parts: what antibiotics clearly prevent, and what to watch for afterward either way.


What antibiotics prevent. The main reason pediatricians treat strep is rheumatic fever, a rare illness that can damage the heart. CDC says treating strep properly is the primary way to prevent it. Antibiotics also lower the chance of the infection spreading to nearby areas, such as an abscess around the tonsils, and they shorten how long your child is sick and contagious. Penicillin and amoxicillin are the usual first-choice medicines, and no strep bacteria have ever been found that resist penicillin (CDC), which is reassuring.


What can happen after strep either way. A kidney problem called post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, which is inflammation of the kidney's filters, can show up about 10 days after a strep infection. CDC says there is not enough evidence to know whether antibiotics prevent it. So in the week or two after strep, watch for dark, reddish-brown urine, puffiness around the eyes, or a big drop in how much your child pees, and call your pediatrician if you see these. More than 9 in 10 children make a full recovery.


## How do you treat strep throat?


Strep throat is treated with an[antibiotic](https://www.blueberrypediatrics.com/knowledge-base/get-antibiotics-online) , usually penicillin or amoxicillin, taken for a full 10 days (CDC). Finish the whole course even after your child feels better, so the infection clears completely.


You can ease symptoms at home while the antibiotics work:


- Offer plenty of fluids, and cold or soft foods that are easy to swallow.
- Use children's acetaminophen or ibuprofen for pain or fever, following the dosing for your child's age and weight.
- Try warm liquids like broth, or honey for children over 1 year old (honey is not safe for babies under 1).
- Gargling with warm salt water can help, but it is only realistic for older children, roughly age 6 and up.
- Let your child rest.


These steps make your child more comfortable, but they do not replace the antibiotics that actually clear the infection.


## Strep in babies, toddlers, and young kids


Strep throat is most common in children 5 through 15 years old and is uncommon under 3, but very young children can still get a strep infection. When they do, it usually does not look like a classic sore throat.


CDC describes strep in children under 3 as thick, gunky nasal discharge, poor eating, crankiness, and a fever that usually is not high. Because strep is rare at this age, pediatricians do not routinely test toddlers who have a sore throat. They will test if there is a reason to, such as an older sibling with confirmed strep, or the sandpaper-like rash of scarlet fever. If a young child does test positive, they are treated with antibiotics like anyone else. In this age group, talk to your pediatrician rather than testing at home.


## How long is strep contagious, and when can my child go back to school?


Once your child starts an appropriate antibiotic, they can go back to school or daycare (here is how[getting a doctor's note](https://www.blueberrypediatrics.com/health-tips/getting-a-doctors-note) works) when all three of these are true (CDC; AAP Red Book):


- They have no fever.
- It has been at least 12 hours since their first dose.
- They are acting well.


All three parts matter, not just the 12 hours.


It usually takes about 2 to 5 days after being around strep to get sick (CDC), which answers the common question, "his classmate has strep, so when would we know?" Without treatment, a person can stay contagious for weeks, which is one more reason to get a sick child tested and treated rather than waiting it out.


## When to seek in-person or emergency care


Most sore throats can be handled at home or with a telemedicine visit, but some signs mean your child needs to be seen in person right away, not tested at home.


Important


Go to in-person care or the ER now, not a telemedicine visit and not a home swab, if your child has trouble breathing, trouble swallowing or is drooling, cannot open their mouth fully, has a stiff or swollen neck, or simply seems very ill. Trouble breathing or extreme trouble swallowing with drooling can signal a more serious infection (AAP). Any baby under 3 months with a fever needs to be seen in person.


Important


Do not skip or stop antibiotics early once strep is confirmed. Finish the full course even after your child feels better, and call your pediatrician if symptoms get worse or do not improve in a couple of days.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### Are at-home strep tests sold over the counter?


Not yet, and there is no legitimate OTC path yet either. Rapid strep tests are prescription-only devices in the US as of August 2026, so getting one always starts with a clinician's order. An online listing marketed as "FDA approved for home use" describes the seller's marketing, not the device's regulatory status; the kits themselves are cleared for clinic use only.


### Can my baby or toddler get strep throat?


Yes, though it is uncommon: strep is most common between ages 5 and 15 and shows up less often before age 3. A younger child with strep usually does not look like the classic sore-throat picture. Think thick, gunky nasal discharge, poor eating, crankiness, and a fever that is often mild rather than high. Pediatricians do not routinely swab toddlers for strep because it is uncommon at this age, though they will test for a specific reason, such as a sibling with confirmed strep or the sandpapery rash of scarlet fever. A positive result in a young child is treated with antibiotics the same as at any other age. In this age group, talk to your pediatrician rather than testing at home.


### What happens if you do not treat strep?


Untreated strep can lead to complications, though they are not common. CDC lists abscesses around the tonsils or in the neck, ear infections, sinus infections, and rheumatic fever (a rare heart complication); treating strep lowers the risk of these. A kidney problem called post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis can also follow a strep infection, though CDC says there is not enough evidence to know whether antibiotics prevent it. This one can happen whether or not strep is treated. Scarlet fever is sometimes confused with a complication, but it is not one. It is simply strep throat plus a sandpapery rash, caused by the same bacteria and treated the same way.


### How accurate is an at-home strep test?


In clinic studies, rapid strep tests catch about 6 out of every 7 cases of strep and rarely give a false positive. But those studies used swabs taken by nurses and doctors. No study has measured how well the test works when a parent swabs at home, so a negative result in a child does not always rule out strep. A Blueberry pediatrician can help guide your next steps.


### How soon after being exposed will symptoms show up?


It usually takes about 2 to 5 days after being around strep to become sick (CDC). If your child was exposed and has no symptoms, watch for a sudden sore throat, fever, and swollen neck glands over that window.


### When can my child go back to school after strep?


Your child can return to school or daycare once they are fever-free, it has been at least 12 hours since their first dose of antibiotics, and they are acting well (CDC). All three need to be true.


### Where can I buy an at-home strep test?


You cannot pick one up off a shelf, since a licensed clinician has to order it first. A Blueberry pediatrician can prescribe a rapid strep test and walk you through swabbing at home, or you can get tested the traditional way at a pediatrician's office, urgent care, or retail clinic.
